section: Section 1: Uṣūl al-Dīn & The Core Sciences (Primary Foundations)

sub_section.name: ʿAqīdah & Kalām (Theology & Creed)
sub_section.description: The foundational beliefs (Uṣūl al-Dīn) of Islām that form the bedrock of faith: Tawḥīd (Oneness of Allāh), ʿAdl (Divine Justice), Nubuwwah (Prophethood), Imāmah (Divine Successorship), and Maʿād (Resurrection and the Afterlife). This sub-section covers the systematic study of Islamic theology (Kalām), including debates on free will vs. predestination (jabr vs. tafwīḍ vs. amr bayn al-amrayn), the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of prophets and Imāms, the nature of the Qurʾān (created or uncreated), divine attributes (ṣifāt), the problem of theodicy, and responses to theological challenges from atheism, materialism, and other faith traditions. Includes classical works by Shaykh al-Mufīd (Awāʾil al-maqālāt), Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (Kitāb al-Tawḥīd), Sharīf al-Murtaḍā (Al-Dhakhīrah), ʿAllāmah al-Ḥillī (Al-Bāb al-ḥādī ʿashar), and modern theological treatises addressing contemporary philosophical challenges to Islamic belief.

sub_section.name: ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān (Qurʾān & Qurʾānic Sciences)
sub_section.description: The comprehensive study of the Holy Qurʾān itself (al-Muṣḥaf) and the sciences related to its revelation, preservation, and transmission. Topics include: revelation (tanzīl) and its gradual descent (tanjīm), the collection and compilation (jamʿ) of the Qurʾān, the arrangement (tartīb) of verses and chapters, the seven and ten canonical recitation styles (qirāʾāt) and their chains of transmission, abrogating and abrogated verses (nāsikh wa mansūkh), the reasons for revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl) — historical contexts behind specific verses, the miraculous nature (iʿjāz) of the Qurʾān — linguistic, scientific, legislative, and prophetic, the clear and allegorical verses (muḥkamāt wa mutashābihāt), the opening letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqāṭṭaʿāt), and the various textual divisions (juzʾ, ḥizb, rubʿ). Includes works on the inimitability of the Qurʾān by al-Bāqillānī and al-Khaṭṭābī, and Shīʿa-specific works on the collection of the Qurʾān. Key works: Al-Tibyān by Shaykh al-Ṭūsī, Al-Burhān fī ʿulūm al-Qurʾān by al-Zarkashī, Al-Itqān by al-Suyūṭī.

sub_section.name: Tafsīr (Exegesis & Commentary)
sub_section.description: Books that explain and interpret the verses of the Qurʾān, uncovering their meanings, legal implications, theological significance, and spiritual depths. Includes both traditional (tafsīr bil-maʾthūr) commentaries that rely on the Prophet's sayings and those of the Imāms, and rational (tafsīr bil-raʾy) commentaries that employ intellectual analysis, linguistic study, and philosophical reasoning. Shīʿa-specific works include Tafsīr al-Mīzān by ʿAllāmah Ṭabāṭabāʾī (a philosophical and Qurʾān-based tafsīr), Tafsīr al-Qummī (early Imāmī tafsīr attributed to ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qummī), Tafsīr al-ʿAskarī (attributed to Imām al-ʿAskarī a.s), Majmaʿ al-Bayān by al-Ṭabrisī (comprehensive and balanced), and Tafsīr al-Ṭūsī (Al-Tibyān). Also includes comparative tafsīrs from other schools like Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr (Sunni), Tafsīr al-Rāzī (rational Sunni), and Tafsīr al-Jalālayn. Includes thematic tafsīr (topic-based), scientific tafsīr, and contemporary tafsīr works addressing modern issues.

sub_section.name: ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth (Ḥadīth & Ḥadīth Sciences)
sub_section.description: Collections of the sayings (aqwāl), actions (afʿāl), and tacit approvals (taqrīrāt) of the Prophet Muḥammad (ṣ.a.w.a) and the 12 Infallible Imāms (a.s). Includes the Four Books (al-Kutub al-Arbaʿah): Al-Kāfī by al-Kulaynī (the most comprehensive), Man lā yaḥḍuruhu al-faqīh by al-Ṣadūq (jurisprudential), Tahdhīb al-aḥkām by al-Ṭūsī (jurisprudential with chains), and Al-Istibṣār by al-Ṭūsī (jurisprudential). Also includes early collections like Baṣāʾir al-darajāt (theological), later encyclopedias like Biḥār al-anwār by al-Majlisī (110 volumes covering all Islamic sciences), Wasāʾil al-shīʿa by al-Ḥurr al-ʿĀmilī (organized by fiqh chapters), Mustadrak al-Wasāʾil, and Saḥīḥat al-Sajjādiyyah (the Psalms of Islām, a collection of supplications from Imām al-Sajjād a.s). Covers the classification of ḥadīth into ṣaḥīḥ (authentic), ḥasan (good), muwaththaq (reliable), ḍaʿīf (weak), and mawḍūʿ (fabricated).

sub_section.name: Rijāl (Biographical Evaluation)
sub_section.description: The science of biographical evaluation (ʿilm al-rijāl) — the systematic documentation of the lives, reliability, and trustworthiness (jarḥ wa taʿdīl) of ḥadīth narrators. This sub-section includes works that categorize narrators by their truthfulness, memory, religious standing, and their connections to the Imāms. Topics include: classifications of narrators into trustworthy (thiqāt), reliable (maqbūl), weak (ḍuʿafāʾ), unknown (majhūl), and fabricators (kadhdhābūn); chains of transmission (asānīd) and their continuity; the teachers and students of each narrator; their birth and death dates; sectarian affiliations; and the historical context of narration. Key works: Rijāl al-Najāshī (the most authoritative Shīʿa rijāl work), Rijāl al-Kashshī (Maʿrifat akhbār al-rijāl — focused on reliability), Fihrist al-Ṭūsī (catalogue of narrators and their books), Muʿjam rijāl al-ḥadīth by al-Khoei (modern 23-volume comprehensive work), Kitāb al-ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn al-Ghaḍāʾirī, and Al-Jarḥ wa al-taʿdīl by Ibn Abī Ḥātim (Sunni reference). Essential for determining the authenticity of ḥadīth.

sub_section.name: Al-Waḍʿ (Fabricated Ḥadīths & Forged Narrations)
sub_section.description: Books dedicated to identifying, exposing, and refuting fabricated (mawḍūʿ) and weak (ḍaʿīf) ḥadīths falsely attributed to the Prophet Muḥammad (ṣ.a.w.a) and the 12 Infallible Imāms (a.s). Topics include: motives for fabrication (political, sectarian, theological, ideological, pious fraud, economic gain); methods of detection (examining chains of transmission for discontinuity or known liars, textual analysis for linguistic anomalies or theological inconsistency, historical anachronisms, contradiction with the Qurʾān and established ḥadīth); famous fabricators (liars, ghulāt/exaggerators, and extremist sects that infiltrated narrations); and collections that compile known forgeries. Includes both Shīʿa-specific works (critiquing narrations in Shīʿa collections, often addressing ghulāt narrations) and comparative studies (fabrications found in Sunni ḥadīth collections like those criticized by Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Albānī). Key works: Al-Mawḍūʿāt by Ibn al-Jawzī (Sunni), Al-Aḥādīth al-mawḍūʿah by al-Albānī (Sunni), Tanzīh al-anbiyāʾ by Sharīf al-Murtaḍā (refuting forged attributions to prophets), and modern Shīʿa works like Dirāsāt fī al-ḥadīth wa al-mawḍūʿāt by al-Shahīd al-Thānī, and critiques of ghulāt narrations in early Shīʿa sources.

sub_section.name: Al-Jawāmiʿ (Comprehensive Fiqh Works)
sub_section.description: Large, multi-volume encyclopedic works that systematically cover all chapters and topics of Islamic jurisprudence (Furūʿ al-Dīn). These comprehensive manuals detail what is wājib (obligatory), ḥarām (forbidden), mustaḥabb (recommended), makrūh (disliked), and jāʾiz (permissible) in every aspect of life — from worship and ritual purity to commercial transactions, family law, and criminal justice. Includes classical works like Al-Muqniʿ by al-Ṣadūq, Al-Intiṣār by Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, Al-Mabsūṭ by Shaykh al-Ṭūsī (the first comprehensive Shīʿa fiqh encyclopedia), Sharāʾiʿ al-Islām by al-Muḥaqqiq al-Ḥillī, Tadhkirat al-fuqahāʾ by al-ʿAllāmah al-Ḥillī, e.t.c.

sub_section.name: ʿIbādāt (Acts of Worship)
sub_section.description: Books focused specifically on devotional acts — the direct servitude (ʿibādah) of a Muslim to Allāh. Topics include: Ṭahārah (ritual purity) — detailed rules for wuḍūʾ (ablution), ghusl (full bath), tayammum (dry ablution), najāsāt (impurities), and muṭahhirāt (purifiers); Ṣalāt (daily prayers) — the five obligatory prayers, their times, conditions, nullifiers, qaḍāʾ (makeup), and recommended prayers (nawāfil); Ṣawm (fasting) — fasting in Ramaḍān, its conditions and nullifiers, and recommended fasts (e.g., ʿArafah, Mondays, Thursdays); Zakāt and Khums — the two obligatory taxes, their rates, niṣāb (thresholds), and distribution; Ḥajj (pilgrimage) and ʿUmrah (lesser pilgrimage) — all rites, conditions, obligatory acts, and prohibitions; Jihād (struggle) — the conditions for defensive and offensive jihad, rules of warfare, and the greater jihad (spiritual struggle against the self). Includes detailed discussions on the intention (niyyah), the spiritual dimensions of worship, and the rulings for special circumstances (travel, illness, emergencies). Key works: Miʿrāj al-kamāl (on salāt), Manāsik al-ḥajj, and extensive chapters in all comprehensive fiqh works.

sub_section.name: Muʿāmalāt (Transactions & Contracts)

sub_section.name: ʿUqūbāt (Penal Law)
sub_section.description: Books on Islamic criminal law — the fixed punishments (ḥudūd) and discretionary penalties for crimes against Allāh and society. Topics include: Ḥudūd (fixed punishments) for specific crimes: adultery/fornication (zinā) — conditions for proof (four witnesses or confession), punishment (stoning for married, flogging for unmarried), and the strict evidentiary standards (to prevent wrongful execution); false accusation of adultery (qadhf) — punishment of 80 lashes for false accusers; theft (sariqah) — punishment of amputation of the hand, conditions (minimum value, necessity, etc.), and the defense of necessity; drinking alcohol (shurb al-khamr) — punishment of 40-80 lashes; apostasy (riddah) — punishment, repentance conditions, and Shīʿa-specific rulings; armed robbery/highway robbery (ḥirābah) — punishment (execution, crucifixion, amputation, exile based on severity). Also covers Qiṣāṣ (retaliation/retribution) — the right of victims to equivalent retribution for murder and bodily harm, including the conditions, rules of intentional vs. unintentional killing, and the victim's family's right to pardon; Diyyah (blood money) — the prescribed compensation for murder and bodily harm, rates based on gender and status, and payment rules; and Taʿzīr (discretionary punishments) — punishments left to the judge's discretion for crimes not covered by ḥudūd or qiṣāṣ. Key works: Kitāb al-ḥudūd in all comprehensive fiqh works, and specialized treatises on Islamic penal law.

sub_section.name: Al-Aḥwāl al-Shakhṣiyyah (Personal Status Law)
sub_section.description: Books on family law and personal status — the Islamic framework for marriage, divorce, inheritance, and familial relationships. Topics include: Marriage (Nikāḥ) — permanent marriage (al-nikāḥ al-dāʾim) conditions, essential elements (offer and acceptance, witnesses), the dower (mahr), forbidden categories of marriage (by blood, marriage, and fosterage), and the rights and responsibilities of spouses; temporary marriage (mutʿah) — its permissibility in Shīʿa Islām, conditions, duration, dower, and its distinction from permanent marriage; Divorce (Ṭalāq) — types (reversible and irreversible), conditions, the waiting period (ʿiddah), the formula of divorce, the role of arbitrators, and the revocability of divorce during the waiting period; Child custody (Ḥiḍānah) — the age until which custody belongs to the mother, conditions for custody transfer, and the father's responsibility for maintenance; Maintenance (Nafaqah) — the obligation of husbands to provide for their wives (food, clothing, shelter) and of fathers for their children; Inheritance (Mīrāth) — the fixed shares (farāʾiḍ) in the Qurʾān, degrees of kinship, the division of estate among heirs, the rules for various family structures (son, daughter, spouse, parents, siblings), the omission of an heir (nawāqid al-irth), and wills and bequests (waṣiyyah) — the maximum allowable bequest (one-third), conditions, and the rules for bequests to non-heirs. Key works: Kitāb al-nikāḥ and Kitāb al-ṭalāq in all comprehensive fiqh works, and modern works on family law reform.

sub_section.name: Aṭʿimah wa Ashribah (Food & Drink)
sub_section.description: Books detailing the Islamic rules for what is permitted (ḥalāl) and forbidden (ḥarām) to consume. Topics include: animals — categories of ḥalāl and ḥarām animals, including land animals (e.g., cattle, sheep, goats, camels, deer are ḥalāl; swine, predatory animals, and some amphibians are ḥarām), birds (e.g., chickens, pigeons are ḥalāl; birds of prey are ḥarām), and sea creatures (all fish with scales and shrimp are ḥalāl in Shīʿa fiqh; shellfish are ḥarām); food and drink — the prohibition of alcohol (khamr) and all intoxicants, rules on consuming items that may contain alcohol (e.g., vanilla extract, kombucha), and the rules for food made by non-Muslims (the People of the Book — their meat may be ḥalāl if properly slaughtered and not containing impurities); the rules for ingredients like gelatin, rennet, and enzymes from animal sources; food additives and modern food processing; eating etiquette (sunnah of eating) — saying Bismillāh, eating with the right hand, moderation, avoiding waste, and gratitude after eating; and the rules for fasting and breaking the fast. Key works: Kitāb al-aṭʿimah wa al-ashribah in all comprehensive fiqh works, and modern ḥalāl certification guides.

sub_section.name: Al-Ṣayd wa al-Dhabāʾiḥ (Hunting & Slaughter)
sub_section.description: Books on the Islamic rules for hunting and ritual slaughter (dhabīḥah) — ensuring that animal-derived food is consumed in a manner compliant with Islamic law. Topics include: The rules of hunting (ṣayd) — permissible animals to hunt, conditions for hunting (using trained animals like falcons or dogs, the use of weapons, ensuring the kill is made by the hunting instrument not by other causes), the requirement to mention Allāh's name at the time of hunting, and the rules for consuming hunted game; The rules of ritual slaughter (dhabḥ) — the conditions for valid slaughter: the slaughterer must be a Muslim or a person of the Book, the animal must be alive at the time of slaughter, the name of Allāh must be mentioned, the throat, windpipe, and jugular veins must be cut, and the animal must be completely drained of blood; The permissibility of meat from the People of the Book (Christians, Jews) and the debates around it; The rules for animals that die naturally (mawt al-tabīʿī) — they are ḥarām unless slaughtered; and modern issues like mechanical slaughter, stunning, and animal welfare. Key works: Kitāb al-ṣayd wa al-dhabāʾiḥ in all comprehensive fiqh works, and contemporary treatises on halal slaughter and industrial food production.

sub_section.name: Ādāb al-Qaḍāʾ (Judicial Etiquette & Court Procedures)
sub_section.description: Books on Islamic legal procedure, judiciary ethics, and court protocols (qaḍāʾ) — the rules for judges, witnesses, evidence, and the administration of justice. Topics include: The qualifications of a judge (qāḍī) — requirements of being a mature, male or female (in Shīʿa fiqh), Muslim, just, knowledgeable in jurisprudence, and capable of independent reasoning (mujtahid); The appointment of judges and the prohibition of seeking judicial appointments; The rules of evidence (bayyināt) — the types of admissible evidence (the Qurʾān, Sunnah, consensus, and reason in legal theory); Witness testimony (shahādah) — the qualifications of witnesses, the number required for different cases (e.g., two male witnesses or one male and two females for financial matters; four male witnesses for adultery), the rejection of testimony, and the punishment for false testimony (qadhf); Oaths (yamīn) — rules for administering oaths, the form of the oath, and their role in judicial proceedings; The procedures of the court (al-adab al-qāḍī) — the etiquette of the courtroom, the conduct of the litigants, and the judge's role in arbitration; The differentiation between personal and public rights; Islamic alternative dispute resolution (al-ṣulḥ); and the relationship between the judiciary and the executive. Key works: Kitāb al-qadāʾ in all comprehensive fiqh works, and specialized treatises on Islamic court procedures.

sub_section.name: Tarīkh (General Islamic History)
sub_section.description: Books documenting the comprehensive history of Islām from the pre-Islamic era (Jāhiliyyah) through the time of the Prophet (ṣ.a.w.a), the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and the great Islamic dynasties — the Umayyads, ʿAbbāsids, Fāṭimids, Ṣafavids, Qājārs, Ottomans, and up to modern times. Topics include: The political, social, and cultural history of Islamic civilization; the rise and fall of dynasties and caliphates; the development of Islamic governance and state structures; major battles, conquests, and political events; the reasons for sectarian divisions and the historical development of the Shīʿa-Sunni schism; the role of the Imāms in history; the influence of Islamic civilization on global history (translation movements, scientific contributions, and cultural transmission); the history of Islamic cities (Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem, Baghdad, Cairo, Isfahan, Qom, Najaf, Karbalā); and the modern history of Islamic states, colonialism, and the Islamic world's engagement with the West. Includes comprehensive works like Tarīkh al-Ṭabarī (the most famous universal history), Murūj al-dhahab by al-Masʿūdī (detailed and engaging history), Al-Kāmil fī al-tarīkh by Ibn al-Athīr, and modern works on Islamic history by scholars like Albert Hourani and Bernard Lewis.
